questions.stem: Which feature allows a molecule to act as a monomer for addition polymerisation?
options: A long chain of single C-C bonds
A carbon-carbon double bond
A hydroxyl group at each end
An amino group and a carboxyl group
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens and the monomers join without losing any atoms. Two reactive groups, such as -OH and -COOH or -NH₂ and -COOH, are what condensation polymerisation needs.

questions.stem: Which monomer could form a condensation polymer on its own?
options: HOCH₂CH₂COOH
CH₂=CHCH₃
CH₃CH₂COOH
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
questions.explanation: HOCH₂CH₂COOH has a hydroxyl group at one end and a carboxyl group at the other, so each molecule can form ester links at both ends, releasing water. Propene forms an addition polymer, and molecules with only one reactive group cannot build a chain.

questions.stem: A section of a polymer is -CH₂-CH(Cl)-CH₂-CH(Cl)-CH₂-CH(Cl)-. What type of polymer is it, and what is its monomer?
options: Addition polymer, made from CH₃CH₂Cl
Condensation polymer, made from CH₂ClCH₂Cl
Addition polymer, made from CH₂=CHCl
Condensation polymer, made from CH₂=CHCl
questions.explanation: The backbone is entirely carbon with no ester or amide links, so it is an addition polymer; the repeating unit -CH₂-CH(Cl)- comes from chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl. Chloroethane has no double bond and cannot add.

questions.stem: A polymer chain contains repeated -CO-NH- groups in its backbone. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is a condensation polymer, and water was released as it formed
It is an addition polymer, and water was released as it formed
It is a condensation polymer, made from monomers with C=C bonds
It is an addition polymer, made from monomers with C=C bonds
questions.explanation: Amide links in the backbone show a polyamide, formed by condensation between amine and carboxylic acid groups with loss of water. Addition polymers have an all-carbon backbone and lose no atoms.

questions.stem: A polyester has the repeating unit -O-CH₂CH₂-O-CO-C₆H₄-CO-. Which pair of monomers forms it?
options: HOCH₂CH₂COOH and HOOC-C₆H₄-OH
CH₂=CH₂ and HOOC-C₆H₄-COOH
HOCH₂CH₂OH and HO-C₆H₄-OH
HOCH₂CH₂OH and HOOC-C₆H₄-COOH
questions.explanation: Each ester link joins an alcohol group to an acid group, so the -O-CH₂CH₂-O- part comes from ethane-1,2-diol and the -CO-C₆H₄-CO- part from a dicarboxylic acid. Two diols cannot form ester links with each other.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of synthetic polymers over traditional materials such as metal, glass and wood?
options: They are light, durable, resist corrosion and are easily moulded
They break down quickly in the environment when they are discarded
They are made only from renewable plant materials such as cellulose
They conduct heat and electricity well, so they are used for wiring
questions.explanation: Low density, durability, resistance to corrosion and ease of moulding make synthetic polymers useful. Most are made from fossil feedstocks, persist in the environment and are electrical insulators, which is why they coat wires rather than form them.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of many synthetic polymers?
options: They are too dense for packaging and add weight and cost to transport
They conduct electricity, so they are a hazard in electrical appliances
They persist in the environment for a long time and can form microplastics
They corrode rapidly in moist air, so they must be painted to protect them
questions.explanation: Most synthetic polymers are not biodegradable, so discarded plastics last for decades and break into small fragments that harm wildlife. They are generally low in density, corrosion-resistant and electrically insulating.

questions.stem: What happens when a thermoplastic polymer and a thermoset polymer are heated strongly?
options: Both soften and can be remoulded many times without changing their structure
Neither softens; both decompose at once because their covalent bonds break
The thermoplastic softens and can be remoulded; the thermoset does not soften
The thermoset softens and can be remoulded; the thermoplastic does not soften
questions.explanation: Thermoplastic chains are held by secondary interactions that weaken on heating, so the chains slide and the plastic softens. A thermoset's chains are joined by covalent cross-links, so it stays rigid until it chars or decomposes.

questions.stem: Why does a thermoset polymer not soften when heated?
options: Its chains contain no carbon atoms, so heat cannot break the interactions
Its chains are joined by many covalent cross-links that do not break on heating
Its chains are held only by dispersion forces, which grow stronger as it heats
Its chains are very short, so there is nothing to slide past each other
questions.explanation: Extensive covalent cross-linking forms a rigid network; the chains cannot slide past each other unless covalent bonds break, which happens only when the polymer decomposes. Dispersion forces weaken, not strengthen, as temperature rises.

questions.stem: Natural rubber is soft and sticky. Heating it with sulfur forms a few sulfur bridges between the chains. Why does this make the rubber stronger but still elastic?
options: The sulfur forms ionic bonds with the rubber, so the material conducts electricity
A few cross-links stop chains sliding apart permanently but still let them stretch
The sulfur bridges replace all secondary interactions, making the chains rigid
The sulfur breaks the chains into shorter pieces that pack together more tightly
questions.explanation: Light cross-linking anchors the chains so they return to shape after stretching instead of flowing; heavy cross-linking would make the material hard and rigid. Vulcanisation adds covalent links, not ionic bonds, and does not shorten the chains.

questions.stem: Two polymers have similar chain lengths. Polymer X has amide groups along its chains; polymer Y is a hydrocarbon. Why is X stronger and higher melting?
options: Covalent bonds within the chains of X are stronger than those within Y
Polymer Y's chains are held together by ionic bonds that break easily
Polymer X has no secondary interactions, so its chains cannot slide
Hydrogen bonds between amide groups on neighbouring chains are stronger
questions.explanation: The N-H and C=O of amide groups form hydrogen bonds between chains, which are much stronger than the dispersion forces between hydrocarbon chains. The bonds within the chains are not what change when a thermoplastic softens.

questions.stem: How does increasing the degree of cross-linking in a polymer change its properties?
options: It becomes softer and more flexible, and melts at a lower temperature
It becomes more soluble in water, as the cross-links attract water
It becomes a better conductor, as electrons travel along cross-links
It becomes more rigid and harder, and less flexible and elastic
questions.explanation: Cross-links tie the chains into a network, so they can move less: the polymer becomes rigid and hard. With extensive cross-linking it becomes a thermoset that does not soften on heating.

questions.stem: Polyethene can be made from ethene obtained from crude oil or from ethanol fermented from sugarcane. Which is a disadvantage of the renewable route?
options: Growing the crop uses farmland, water and fertiliser that could produce food
The polyethene made from sugarcane has a different structure and is weaker
Sugarcane ethene contains no carbon, so it cannot be polymerised at all
The sugarcane route releases more fossil carbon than the crude oil route
questions.explanation: The polymer is identical whichever source of ethene is used, and plant feedstock reduces the use of finite fossil resources. But the crop competes for land, water and fertiliser, and processing still uses energy.

questions.stem: Polyethene made from sugarcane ethanol is sometimes described as biodegradable because it comes from plants. Why is this claim wrong?
options: It contains sulfur cross-links from the sugarcane that resist bacterial attack
Its structure is the same as fossil polyethene, with a C-C backbone microbes rarely break
Plant-based polymers never biodegrade because they contain no ester or amide links
It is a thermoset, so microorganisms cannot reach the chains to break them
questions.explanation: Biodegradability depends on structure, not origin. Bio-based polyethene is chemically identical to fossil polyethene, whose long C-C chains resist breakdown by microorganisms. Some plant-based polymers with ester links do biodegrade.

questions.stem: Why are polymers such as polylactic acid (PLA), which have ester links in the backbone, more biodegradable than polyethene?
options: Ester links are much stronger than C-C bonds, so microorganisms digest them first
Ester links can be hydrolysed, so microorganisms can break the chains into small molecules
Ester links absorb sunlight strongly, so the chains burn away when exposed outdoors
Ester links make the polymer soluble in water, so it washes away in the rain
questions.explanation: The ester links can be hydrolysed, including by microbial enzymes, breaking the chain into small molecules that organisms can use. An all-carbon backbone has no such weak point.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of using biodegradable polymers for items such as food packaging?
options: They break down after disposal, reducing litter and the volume of landfill
They last indefinitely in the environment, so they can be reused forever
They are always stronger and more heat-resistant than other polymers
They release no carbon dioxide at all when they break down after use
questions.explanation: Biodegradable polymers are broken down by microorganisms after use, so they do not persist as litter or occupy landfill for decades. Their breakdown does release CO₂, and they are often less durable than conventional plastics.

questions.stem: Why are gold and silver found uncombined in nature, while sodium and aluminium are found only in compounds?
options: Gold and silver are unreactive, while sodium and aluminium react readily
Gold and silver are reactive, while sodium and aluminium are unreactive
Gold and silver are denser, so their compounds sink and break apart
Gold and silver have higher melting points than their compounds
questions.explanation: Metals low in the activity series have little tendency to lose electrons, so they survive as the element. Reactive metals have lost electrons to form ions in oxides, chlorides, carbonates and silicates.

questions.stem: Zinc sulfide ore is roasted in air before the zinc is extracted: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. What is the purpose of this step?
options: To dissolve the zinc sulfide so that the impurities can be filtered
To oxidise the zinc ions to a higher oxidation state before smelting
To convert the sulfide into an oxide that can be reduced more easily
To reduce the zinc ions in the ore directly to zinc metal
questions.explanation: Roasting converts the mineral into zinc oxide, a form suitable for reduction by carbon, or for dissolving in acid before electrolysis. Zinc stays as Zn²⁺ throughout roasting; it is the sulfide ion that is oxidised, to SO₂.

questions.stem: In a blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Why can carbon monoxide be used to extract iron but not aluminium?
options: Aluminium is too reactive for carbon to remove the oxygen from its oxide
Aluminium oxide is a gas at furnace temperatures, so it escapes unreacted
Aluminium is less reactive than iron, so its oxide decomposes without carbon
Carbon monoxide reacts with aluminium to form a carbonate instead of the metal
questions.explanation: Carbon can reduce oxides of metals of moderate reactivity, such as iron, zinc and lead. Aluminium holds oxygen too strongly, so its oxide must be electrolysed instead. Aluminium is above iron, not below it, in the activity series.

questions.stem: Which method is used to obtain sodium metal from sodium chloride?
options: Heating sodium chloride in a stream of air
Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride
Electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride
Heating sodium chloride with carbon
questions.explanation: Sodium is very reactive, so carbon cannot reduce its compounds, and in aqueous solution water is reduced to hydrogen at the cathode instead of Na⁺. Electrolysis of the molten salt gives sodium at the cathode.

questions.stem: Using the activity series K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au, which pairing of metal and likely extraction method is correct?
options: Gold: electrolysis of its molten oxide in a cell
Lead: reduction of its oxide by heating with carbon
Sodium: reduction of its chloride by heating with carbon
Potassium: electrolysis of an aqueous solution of KCl
questions.explanation: Lead is of moderate reactivity, so carbon can reduce its oxide. Sodium is far too reactive for carbon to reduce its compounds, potassium cannot be deposited from water, and gold occurs uncombined so needs no reduction.

questions.stem: Copper can be produced by electrolysis of an aqueous solution of copper(II) sulfate. Why does this work for copper but not for sodium?
options: Na⁺ is reduced more readily than water, but water is reduced before Cu²⁺
Copper(II) sulfate is soluble in water, but sodium compounds are insoluble
Copper is more reactive than sodium, so its ions gain electrons more easily
Cu²⁺ is reduced more readily than water, but water is reduced before Na⁺
questions.explanation: At the cathode, the species most easily reduced reacts first. Cu²⁺ ions of an unreactive metal accept electrons more readily than water, so copper is deposited; for sodium, water is reduced to hydrogen instead. Sodium salts are generally soluble.

questions.stem: Aluminium can be made by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide; iron is made by reducing its oxide with carbon. Which statement compares the two methods correctly?
options: Electrolysis releases no greenhouse gases, whatever the source of its electricity
Carbon reduction gives purer metal because no carbon dioxide is formed
Carbon reduction is used for aluminium in places where electricity is costly
Electrolysis needs large amounts of electricity, making aluminium costly to produce
questions.explanation: Melting the oxide and supplying enough current for electrolysis uses a great deal of electrical energy, so aluminium smelters are sited where electricity is relatively cheap. Emissions depend on how the electricity is generated, and carbon reduction always produces CO₂.

questions.stem: In an electrolytic cell, which statement about the electrodes is correct?
options: The cathode is positive and is where reduction occurs
The cathode is negative and is where oxidation occurs
The anode is positive and is where oxidation occurs
The anode is negative and is where oxidation occurs
questions.explanation: Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. In an electrolytic cell the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the power supply, the reverse of a galvanic cell, where the anode is negative.

questions.stem: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved before it can be electrolysed?
options: Its ions must be heated above their boiling points
Its ions must be free to move to the electrodes
Its electrons must be free to move through the liquid
Its covalent bonds must break so the atoms separate
questions.explanation: In the solid the ions are fixed in a lattice; melting or dissolving lets cations migrate to the cathode and anions to the anode, carrying the current. Electrons do not travel through the electrolyte.

questions.stem: What supplies the energy that drives the reaction in an electrolytic cell?
options: An external power supply, such as a DC source
The spontaneous reaction between the electrodes
Heat released as the molten electrolyte cools
A salt bridge connecting the two half-cells
questions.explanation: The reactions in an electrolytic cell are not spontaneous, so a power supply must push electrons onto the cathode and draw them from the anode. A spontaneous reaction producing a current describes a galvanic cell.

questions.stem: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. Which is the half-equation at the cathode?
options: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
questions.explanation: The cathode is negative and attracts Na⁺ ions, which gain electrons to form liquid sodium. Chloride ions are oxidised to chlorine gas at the anode.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, how do the ions and electrons move?
options: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ both move to the cathode; electrons flow through the molten salt to the anode
Na⁺ moves to the cathode, Cl⁻ to the anode; electrons flow through the molten salt itself
Na⁺ moves to the cathode, Cl⁻ to the anode; electrons flow from anode to cathode in the wire
Na⁺ moves to the anode, Cl⁻ to the cathode; electrons flow from cathode to anode in the wire
questions.explanation: Cations move to the negative cathode and anions to the positive anode. Electrons released at the anode travel through the external circuit, pushed by the power supply, to the cathode; electrons do not travel through the electrolyte.

questions.stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Copper forms at the cathode and a gas is given off at the anode. Which is the anode half-equation?
options: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻
2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: At the anode, water is oxidised to oxygen gas, leaving the solution more acidic. Sulfate ions are not oxidised under these conditions, and 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻ is a reduction, which happens at a cathode.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide, which half-equation occurs at the cathode?
options: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻
O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻
Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
questions.explanation: Aluminium ions are reduced at the negative cathode, gaining three electrons each. Oxide ions are oxidised to oxygen at the anode, where the oxygen also reacts with the carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How do an electrolytic cell and a galvanic cell differ?
options: An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction
An electrolytic cell produces electrical energy from a spontaneous reaction
In a galvanic cell, oxidation happens at the cathode and reduction at the anode
In a galvanic cell, electrons flow through the electrolyte between electrodes
questions.explanation: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy from a spontaneous reaction, while an electrolytic cell uses a power supply to force a reaction that would not occur on its own. In both, oxidation is at the anode, and electrons move only through the external circuit.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of recycling aluminium cans instead of producing new aluminium from ore?
options: It avoids the need to separate cans from other household waste
It turns the aluminium into a renewable resource that grows back
It uses far less energy and conserves the finite supply of ore
It produces aluminium that is more reactive than the original metal
questions.explanation: Remelting aluminium needs only a small fraction of the energy needed to extract it from aluminium oxide by electrolysis, and it reduces mining and waste. Recycling does not change the metal's chemistry, and ore does not regenerate.

questions.stem: Why are thermoplastic polymers much easier to recycle than thermoset polymers?
options: Thermosets are made from renewable materials that cannot be heated
Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded; thermosets cannot
Thermosets dissolve in water, so they are lost during the washing stage
Thermoplastics contain covalent cross-links that hold their shape when melted
questions.explanation: Because their chains are held by secondary interactions, thermoplastics can be melted and formed into new products. The covalent cross-links of thermosets prevent melting, so heating only decomposes them.

questions.stem: Which of these is a composite material?
options: Carbon-fibre reinforced polymer
Pure aluminium
High-density polyethene
Copper(II) sulfate
questions.explanation: A composite combines two or more constituent materials to give properties neither has alone: here strong carbon fibres in a polymer matrix give a light, very strong, stiff material. The others are single substances.

questions.stem: Why is carbon-fibre reinforced polymer used in racing cars and bicycle frames?
options: It combines high strength and stiffness with low density
It conducts heat well, so the frame cools down quickly
It is easily melted down and recycled after each season
It is cheaper than steel and is made from renewable material
questions.explanation: The carbon fibres provide strength and stiffness and the polymer binds them, giving a material much lighter than steel for the same strength. It is expensive and, being a composite, difficult to recycle.

questions.stem: Why are composite materials, and objects such as padded envelopes made of paper and plastic bubble wrap, difficult to recycle?
options: Their different materials are bonded together and hard to separate for processing
Each material in them is a thermoset, which cannot be melted or reused at all
They contain toxic metals that must be removed by electrolysis before recycling
Their materials react with each other when heated, forming new polymers
questions.explanation: Recycling processes handle one material at a time, so components with different properties must first be separated, which is costly or impossible when they are bonded or mixed. Paper and many plastics in such objects could be recycled on their own.
